title: Yayla çorbası
subtitle: Turkish yoghurt and rice soup with dried mint
excerpt: Yayla corbasi is a pale, tangy Turkish soup built on yoghurt, rice, and a finish of dried-mint butter. It is the opposite of heavy, yet it is deeply satisfying. The name means highland soup, and it has the clean, cool flavour of somewhere high up and away from everything.
sourceNotes: A Turkish yoghurt soup common across Anatolia. The mint-butter finish is essential; without it the soup tastes incomplete.

recipe.freezeNotes: Yoghurt soups do not freeze well. The yoghurt separates on thawing.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Reheat very gently; do not boil or the yoghurt will curdle.

content.text: Yayla corbasi is a mild, tangy yoghurt soup thickened with rice and lifted by a spoonful of mint-infused butter at the end. It is eaten all across Turkey and is particularly associated with the pastoral highlands, where yoghurt and rice were the ingredients always to hand.

The key to a smooth result is tempering the yoghurt before it goes into the hot stock. Beat in a little flour and an egg yolk, then ladle some of the hot stock into the yoghurt slowly before combining everything. This prevents curdling and keeps the soup pale and silky.
Once it is done, heat is the enemy: the soup must never boil again. Serve straight away or keep warm over the lowest possible heat.
Bring the stock to the boil in the large pan. Add the rice and salt, reduce the heat to a steady simmer, and cook for 15 minutes until the rice is tender.

While the rice cooks, whisk the yoghurt, flour, and egg yolk together in a large bowl until smooth. Ladle two or three spoonfuls of the hot stock into the yoghurt bowl, whisking constantly after each addition. This brings the yoghurt up to temperature gradually so it will not separate when combined with the soup.

Pour the tempered yoghurt into the soup pan in a steady stream, stirring constantly. Heat gently over a medium-low heat until the soup is hot but not boiling; boiling will curdle it. Taste and adjust the salt. For the mint butter, melt the butter in the small pan, stir in the dried mint and Aleppo pepper, and pour a little over each bowl.

rows.cause: Yoghurt added too fast or soup brought to the boil
rows.fix: Always temper the yoghurt first and never boil once combined. The flour helps stabilise it.

rows.symptom: Rice too thick at the bottom
rows.fix: Stir well before serving; the rice settles quickly. Add a splash of hot water to loosen if needed.
Use a good stock and season generously. The mint butter at the end is essential for flavour.

content.text: Replace the rice with fine bulgur wheat for a nuttier version. Some cooks add a handful of cooked chickpeas for extra body. The soup can also be finished with dried thyme instead of mint for a different herbal note.
The soup keeps for up to 2 days in the fridge. Reheat very gently and never let it boil. Make the mint butter fresh when serving.

Yayla corbasi comes from the highlands of central and eastern Anatolia, where dairy and grain are the staples. You find it on restaurant menus next to mercimek corbasi, and at home it is a quiet midweek supper in a bowl.
